chapters.summary: Council staff opens the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use hearing, asks attendees to silence devices, fill out testimony slips, and not approach the desk. The chair is told the committee is ready to begin.
chapters.title: Staff gives hearing instructions and asks attendees to silence devices

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to the New York City High Bed hearing on the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please silent all electronic devices at this time.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Also, if you have not yet filled out a testimony slip, please do that with a sergeant at arms in the back of the room or outside in the foyer.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Also, please do not approach the desk.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your kind cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, we are ready to begin.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Tiffany Caban, Chair of the New York City's Council's Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you all for joining us at this oversight hearing on syringe litter management and related support services.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We will also be hearing three pieces of legislation, Intro 67, sponsored by Councilmember David Carr, establishing a public outreach and education campaign regarding the availability and use of fentanyl test strips.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: RESO 262, sponsored by Councilmember Linda Lee, calling on New York State to mandate basic training in addiction treatment as a requirement for medical schools that receive state funding.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And RESO 263, also sponsored by Councilmember Lee, calling on the federal government to mandate basic training in addiction treatment as a requirement for medical schools that receive federal funding.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We have been joined by Council Members Felder, Aldeball, Hankerson, Wilson, Lee, and Carr.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: There are very real public health concerns from discarded syringes that should be recognized, especially in a place as dense as New York City.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The risk that they pose shouldn't be minimized.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Parents shouldn't have to sweep a playground before their kids can play.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Workers shouldn't fear a needle stick on the job.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: In 2024 alone, outreach teams picked up nearly 200,000 syringes up off of our streets.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But today's hearing is about much more than litter.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's about the story that is told behind each syringe and discarded needle and the very real humans behind them.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Because behind every syringe use is a person, someone's child, parent, or neighbor.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And often someone whose substance use disorder began with a prescription, with trauma, with pain that our systems left untreated.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And too often we met them with handcuffs instead of help.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Arrests, evictions, lost jobs, lost children, weeks-long waits for treatment, and so much shame that people hide.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Nearly half of all deaths among homeless New Yorkers in the most recent reporting year were caused by drugs or alcohol.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that's not a personal failing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It is a policy failure.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that failure does not fall on everyone equally.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We've made some real progress.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Overdose deaths fell from 2023 to 2024, but still six New Yorkers die every single day.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Black and Latino New Yorkers die of overdose at twice the rate of white New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Black New Yorkers have the highest overdose death rate of any group in our city, and the highest rates are among black New Yorkers in their late 50s and early 60s, which is, quite frankly, a group that's too often left out of how we treat.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: talk about this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Men die at roughly three times the rate of women.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The Bronx has the highest overdose death rate of any borough, and Hunts Point, Mott Haven, Highbridge, Morrisania, and Crotona-Tremont have among the highest rates in the city.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: In 2023, the rate in Hunts Point, Mott Haven was more than triple the citywide average.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And these aren't accidents of geography.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: They're the result of decades of disinvestment, over-policing, and structural racism in the very neighborhoods where the crisis is now the worst.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The Community Syringe Redemption Program was built to meet both of those realities.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It was created by local law through this council and launched in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It trains participants to safely collect used syringes and return them to mobile vans in eight high-need neighborhoods for 20 cents a syringe up to $10 a day.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: More than 2 million syringes have now been safely collected and disposed of.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Just as important, the program brings people into contact with care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Every participant is trained not only in safe syringe handling, but in how to respond to an overdose and administer naloxone so that the people who are out on our streets every day are equipped to save a life.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Because participants come back to the vans week after week, the program builds something our system too often lacks, a regular, trusted, low-barrier point of contact with people who may never walk into a clinic.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so at each visit, staff can connect people to nearby syringe service programs, which offer naloxone, HIV and hepatitis C testing, drug testing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: drug checking, counseling, and pathways to treatment and other health and social services.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: For someone who has been failed by every system that they have touched, a relationship that starts with $10 and a conversation can be the first door back to care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Clean streets and saved lives are not competing goals.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: A city that is serious about public health has to be serious about public space and serious about the people that we have failed.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to thank the administration for being here, as well as the committee staff and my staff that helped prepare for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I look forward to today's testimony.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And actually, with that, I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Carr, who has a statement.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for your leadership on these issues and, of course, this committee.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's an important, very important issue facing every one of our boroughs.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: An average person, an average one person dies every five hours from a drug overdose in our city.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And the vast majority of these, nearly 80%, are caused by fentanyl.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Fentanyl is not only mixed in with other illicit drugs to increase potency, it's also sold as powders and nasal sprays and increasingly pressed into pills to make it look like legitimate prescription drugs.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Not just opioids, but also anti-anxiety and antidepressants like Xanax and Ativan.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: A lethal dose of fentanyl can be the equivalent to just a few grains of table salt.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And this minute amount can be detected by test strips that our city already distributes for free.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: This legislation would simply require a public education campaign to take place to make people aware that these fentanyl test strips are available and to use them.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: We need to do much more to stop the scourge of addiction that is afflicting our city and to encourage people to get the treatment that they need.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But we can't help them unless we keep them alive.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And we need these test strips to help do just that.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And, you know, the chair was talking about the numbers in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And the reality is that this is a scourge that is affecting every community in our city, every borough, and frankly, the nation.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: There's no part of this country that's been left untouched, and we need to do everything that we can to tackle this crisis together.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I want to thank the chair again for hearing this bill today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I want to thank Majority Leader Abreu and Councilmember Lewis for already signing on as co-sponsors.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I also want to thank our former colleague, now State Senator Eric Botcher, who was the original prime sponsor of this bill last term.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I urge my colleagues to support it.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Now I'm going to turn it over to the committee counsel to administer the oath to the representatives from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Now in accordance with the rules of the council, I will minister the affirmation to the witnesses from the mayoral administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin when ready.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: All right, thanks.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Let's see if I can handle both looking at this and then looking at all of you.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Caban and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I'm Dr.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Rebecca Lynn Walton, Assistant Commissioner for the Bureau of Alcohol and Drug Use at the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, the Health Department.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: On behalf of Commissioner Martin, I thank you for the opportunity to testify today about our efforts to safely collect and dispose of syringe litter, our contracted syringe service providers,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: and the outreach and syringe litter teams that connect individuals to the support services they may need.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I'm joined by Assistant Chief Frank Lattera from the New York City Department of Sanitation, DSNY.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Overdose deaths decreased by 28% in New York City from 2023 to 2024.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: While this sustained decrease is promising, overdose continues to be a public health emergency, and there are substantial inequities in overdose deaths across demographic and geographic groups in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: In particular, overdose deaths remain disproportionately high among black and Latino New Yorkers, residents of the Bronx, and residents of neighborhoods with very high levels of poverty.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The decline in overdose deaths that we have seen reflects persistent but often unseen efforts by community advocates, harm reductionists, and care providers, and follows significant city investments across the substance use continuum of care.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Syringe service providers, SSPs, are a critical component of New York City's overdose response strategy and are an invaluable resource.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: source for the safe collection and disposal of syringes.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: SSPs are community-based organizations designated as New York State Licensed Syringe Exchange Programs, SEPs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: To fulfill their duties as state-licensed SEPs, SSPs offer access to sterile syringes and safe syringe disposal.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Some have dedicated teams to collect and safely dispose of used syringes found in the communities they serve.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The Health Department contracts with all 14 syringe service programs in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: They provide syringes and reduce community spread of infectious disease, along with a myriad of other essential services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I'll refer to this network of 14 community-based organizations as SSPs going forward.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: SSPs also provide a range of health services, including referrals to on-site physical and mental health care, opioid use

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: disorder treatment with buprenorphine, naloxone distribution, overdose education, HIV and hepatitis C testing and counseling, drug treatment counseling, support groups, drop-in centers, and in some cases, outreach and syringe litter teams.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Harm reduction services offered by SSPs provide key opportunities for connections to care and work in tandem with other components of substance use care spectrum, such as treatment and recovery services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The health department remains committed to the safe collection and disposal of syringes.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: To date, in 2026, January through August, outreach and syringe litter teams collected and safely

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: disposed of more than 46,000 ground syringes, provided syringe disposal education and materials in over 8,200 encounters,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: distributed over 7,800 naloxone kits, initiated over 18,000 participant engagements, and made more than 8,300 referrals to additional care services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Thanks to the City Council, the Health Department launched our Community Syringe Redemption Program last spring.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: This was a novel addition to our layered approach to addressing syringe litter in parks and other spaces in New York City where complaints were highest.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The Redemption Program is designed to reduce syringe litter by allowing participants to return used syringes to the program for a small financial incentive.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: This encourages proper disposal and simultaneously serves as a low-threshold engagement opportunity for people who use drugs to be connected to services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: This program also refers participants to SSPs and other services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Since its launch in March 2025, the Community Syringe Redemption Program has collected over 3.5 million syringes and enrolled over 2,400 participants across just eight sites in Queens, Manhattan, Brooklyn, and the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The Health Department recognizes the public safety and quality of life issues associated with syringe litter.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: This is a growing concern that the Mamdani administration takes seriously.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: We are working closely with our partners in Parks Department, DSNY, and other city agencies to address syringe litter.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: DSNY provides needle collection in high-need areas, particularly in the city.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: around schools, transit stops, and public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: This collection is done during daily needle patrols, responding to 311 complaints, and through interagency encampment cleanups.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: DSNY services certain hotspots daily or multiple times a week and has collected nearly 40,000 needles so far this year.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Many people use syringes for a range of medical and health needs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: It is important for New Yorkers to know how to properly dispose of needles, and we will use this opportunity to educate everyone tuning in.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Needles and other sharps should be placed in sharps containers or other leak-proof, puncture-resistant containers such as laundry detergent bottles and sealed and labeled with home sharps, not for recycling.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: These containers can be brought to a collection site, a map can be found on DSNY's website, or discarded as trash.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there has been an increase in the number of sanitation workers struck by needles in recent years.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: DSNY recently finalized a rule to increase the penalty for improper disposal of needles from $100 to $250 to discourage this dangerous practice.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Before I answer your questions, I'd like to briefly discuss the legislation being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Introduction 67 will require the health commissioner to establish an ongoing public outreach and educational campaign regarding the use and availability of fentanyl test strips.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The health department supports this legislation and currently provides extensive public outreach and education on the availability and use of fentanyl test strips.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The department offers regularly scheduled virtual public trainings twice a month and multiple resources on fentanyl test strips on our website.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: These resources include an instructional video, brochure, and poster available in multiple languages, and also includes information on locations where the public can access fentanyl test strips.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: In 2026 thus far, the Health Department has already distributed over 118,000 fentanyl test strips to community-based providers.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: More information in our efforts to engage the public and educate individuals around the accessibility of fentanyl test strips is available on NYC Health's Alcohol and Drug Use Services page.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: There are a few points within the bill language we would like to clarify, and we look forward to discussing the bill further.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The Health Department remains committed to partnership with the Council and other community stakeholders to find more solutions for the safe collection and disposal of syringe litter and its impact on community quality of life.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today, and I look forward to answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Does sanitation have separate testimony?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Great, we'll dive in.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I just want to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Areola on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm gonna start with just a few questions, give it to my colleagues, and then I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But we'll start sort of on the basics.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Wanna know the scale of the problem, how it's currently being measured,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: How do you currently measure the amount of syringe litter in public spaces?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So, for example, is it through a combination of 311 complaints?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is it through DOHMH outreach and litter team counts?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is it through CSRP returns?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Where are you guys getting that number from?

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: So I'll start with 311s.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: 311S primarily come to sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: We have our needle crews out there 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: So when the 311s come in, and let me just clear that up, it's 311s for all city streets, sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: We handle everything except inside a park.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: Inside a park, we will reroute that to the parks department.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: We have crews 24-7, seven days a week.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: We try to expedite, especially if it's near a school or near, if there's other homeless encampments around there, we're going to try to expedite and get there a little bit quicker.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: We usually are out there within four to five hours, sometimes even quicker, but we respond to every 311 within hours.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: We also keep track of every single needle we pick up.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then do you take those numbers and combine them with a different set of numbers?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Or come from different places?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Oh, and before you answer that, I just want to say, one, it's nice to have you here.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Obviously, you're not a regular player in our committee's testimony.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And Councilmember Gutierrez says that your folks do a really great job doing syringe pickup before school starts nearby.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I just wanted to say thank you on her behalf.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: Appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: There's many schools that we are out there before, schools that have a needle epidemic around them, where we try to get out there before the kids arrive.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, and how the health department adds to that is through a wide variety of our syringe abatement programs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So we have the syringe service, the syringe redemption program.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: We also work with parks very closely because they have their kiosks and then we have

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: have the syringe service programs service them.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so they add that to their needle collection figures that they're sharing out as well.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And we collect both information about the syringe service programs, how much they're collecting on site, but then also the outreach syringe litter team.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So only five SSPs right now have it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And from those, they're able to pick up hundreds of thousands of syringes a year.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And as a follow-up to that, out of all of the areas that you're getting data or numbers in terms of syringe pickup, is there anybody doing pickup that you're currently not able to get the numbers from?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, so we also, so across, sorry, my kid gave me a cold like three weeks ago and I'll be coughing for the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if you need tissues, we can get you tissues.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Let us know.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Nope, I'm just going to be coughing for the rest of the season.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So we also work with, so we have 14 syringe service programs across all five boroughs, so they don't cover all of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we regularly are talking to people at OCMH.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: We'll be talking to community partners and talking about how they can safely pick up syringes.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So maybe we don't get a syringe count from them, but we're understanding and elected share with us hotspots that they're noticing.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so from all of that, we're trying to get a picture of where we should put our efforts.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So maybe it won't be like I'll have a number of in Sunset Park, for example, they have this many syringes, but we know it's an issue.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we're working together with our sister agencies to address it.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The hotspots, like what, which neighborhoods are carrying the heaviest syringe litter?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then how does that correspond with where harm reduction services are?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, so how we picked the eight sites for the syringe redemption program was we looked at 311 complaints, and we're really grateful for open data, and then also complaints we were getting from council members.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So those eight sites are actually the highest volume of syringe litter we're noticing, so like the Hub in the South Bronx, Echo Park, St.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Mary's Park, although I have to say St.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Mary's Park is tremendously much cleaner now as a result of all of the efforts going on, but still a long way to go.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we also at Walter Gladwin Park, so it's a South Bronx, it's Upper Manhattan, Midtown is an issue as well.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: But also then we'll notice other neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I keep mentioning Sunset Park just because that hasn't historically been an area that we've had these services in.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: But that's one of the areas that we had outreach from council members in the community.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's where we're working with the community.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: The hotspots are going to be familiar to all of you because it's often where public drug use is highest and the overdose rates are highest.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's where we've really been focusing our efforts as the health department and then in partnership with other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: Counting the year 23, we were at 23.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: Calendar year 22, we're at 25.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: And calendar year 21, we were at 29.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: So we're up significantly with, you know, two full months to go.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So questions I have.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: You know, obviously we want to, oh, I have a quick follow-up, and then I'll go to Councilmember Aldewall on that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Obviously, we want to reduce the number of syringes on the street so that there isn't an opportunity to get stuck.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: In the meantime, while you're seeing this increase, will there be adjustments to maybe more frequent training on proper and safe disposal, things like that, to reduce the number of sticks that you're seeing in the department?

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: Yeah, so Commissioner Anderson has done some social media campaigns with the health commissioner, I believe, and other people from city council getting out there doing some social media campaigns on how people could properly dispose of.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: We're doing some mail outs and other follow ups.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Councilmember Aldewall?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: According to your third quarter report, fentanyl, and you mentioned it in your statement, fentanyl consistently remains involved in the majority of overdose deaths citywide.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The Bronx has remained.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The most susceptible of all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Since you issued your report, have you altered your mode of operation in these particularly vulnerable communities?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And how are you using your data collection tools to decide where to place naloxone distribution, for example?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And I would say we use every quarter data to see how we need to adjust it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: We absolutely agree, and we really try to take a zero overdose.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: approach because we don't want any single overdose.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So one of the programs we're really proud of that we launched over the summer was a community ambassador program.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: We looked at the 10 highest zip codes of overdose deaths and we had people hired from the community to go do naloxone training and many people said that they had heard of naloxone but had never received a kit and so we really were trying to reach the people who

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: You know, we've initially blanketed the city with naloxone as much as possible, but then you have to do targeted in-reach to communities.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Happy to work with you and your community as well.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And we really rely on electeds and community folks to let us know there's an issue in my neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: That's why we wound up doing naloxone training for home health workers as well.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And we really do try to constantly be changing our approach in terms of what's evidence-based to better in-reach to communities that we haven't hit before.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Because you don't want any New Yorkers to be dying of an overdose.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And what existing outreach models does the department have to reach those who may be hesitant to look for help?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, so we have a bunch of different outreach techniques because we recognize that we want it to be a lot of different ways.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So we have, I have a couple really, or a few really fabulous folks in my community, in my department who are going out.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: We also, that's why we engage with the syringe service programs because they have a lot of people with very deep lived experience in a wide variety of ways to be going out into their own communities to be doing outreach and then doing things like driving someone back to on point.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: or Satcher or Harlem United or any of them with a drop-in center so that they are not in public using and they are able to access supports.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And we also work with a tremendous number of treatment providers as well, as well as work very closely with OASIS

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: so that we can recognize that, you know, I'm an example of someone who was sent to treatment and it was incredibly effective, but I was also told at this incredibly effective treatment that within a year, only two of us would still be in recovery and within five years, half of us would be dead.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so I always use that as an example of if it doesn't work, if that doesn't work for you, you could be dead.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we always want to make sure we're having as many doors as possible for people to get into.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's why the syringe service programs have been great about getting people on medication for opioid use disorder and also traditional treatment.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And that's why OASIS and we have rolled out additional funding for recovery centers as well.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: How much of your budget is allocated towards the OSL and SSPs?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So I can get back to you with the actual figures.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I will say that we provide a wide range of both traditional treatment funding.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I would say it's evenly spread for the number of programs across the city.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then we also work with the state to make sure they have resources.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: One more?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I know I have a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So the fiscal management, the 2026 fiscal management reports, the mayor's management report indicates that needles removed by DSNY fell.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: 49% after three consecutive years of increases.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, DSNY attributed this loss to the decline in interagency cleanup operations.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Staff was appropriated to address other operations.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Is there any outreach or interagency cooperation happening now to confront this decline?

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I think the decline can be...

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: There's a lot of different factors.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I think the Department of Health is out there a lot more than they've ever been.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I think they picked up over 3.5 million syringes.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I think you have a lot of these little pop-up agencies.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I know last year when we started in the hub, it seemed like there were little pop-up agencies coming out of the woodwork to help us with syringe pickup.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: They were there around the clock, so I think they had a big part in it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I think the winter weather of three months of not being out there, January, February, and almost most of March, had a lot to do with the decline.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: So I think there's a lot of factors.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I know that DHS and DSS is out there every single day assessing every single homeless New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: So I think the decline is really about what happened in the past months.

utterances.speaker: Frank Lattera
utterances.text: I think you'll see the increase come again.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We can talk offline about the East Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I just want to go back to the report for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So the report, it doesn't have participant demographics, right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It's not including race, ethnicity, gender, housing status, prior SSP enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is DOHMH collecting this?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if so, will you share it?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So we don't for this program, and it's because the way it is designed is to be the lightest touch of all of our interventions.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so I honestly can tell you that for many months, some people will not talk to us during an exchange.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we don't want to do anything to deter them from being willing to come and hand in syringes.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I will say that over time, people then do talk to us.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And I was out at Walter Gladwin Park on Monday.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so someone was sharing that they love this.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then we had like a crowd of people coming to tell me that they love this program.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so those are folks that, and then one of the people was interviewing for a job that day and he had been a participant.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so, you know, I think it's really important to have information about the people we're serving unless it's going to stop them from coming for those services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so while we try to, the same for our syringe service programs, that's also a lighter touch.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so if you want someone to access treatment for infectious disease, then you have to make it as easy as possible.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: That's why we have a lot more data on the traditional treatment setting type because that's much higher.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Barriers to get into and or takes more to access that system and so that's why we have more robust information about them related to being as as low touch as as possible right now participants they sign a liability waiver

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: covering AR, DOHMH and all the partners why is the waiver required and do you sense that

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: discourages anybody from enrolling at all?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: It really doesn't because we're doing so much education around safe pickup.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And once you get the hang of safely picking up, like I've never injured myself and ARR, the people who've been operating for years in Boston, and now we're lucky enough to work with them, they've never had needle stick injuries.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's why it's so important to be handing out those materials and they hand out the disposal cups so that people can, it fits about 50 syringes.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so people are just putting it in there and then they know to hand that in.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then we're really trying to avoid as much opportunities to get hurt as possible.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So we haven't found it to be a deterrent.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You spoke about this a little bit in terms of conversations that happen.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Sometimes they do, sometimes they don't.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Sometimes it takes time.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What is the scope of the things that can happen at a redemption visit beyond the exchange?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I know you said for a little while a lot of people might not want to engage at all, but is every participant at least offered a service conversation or offered naloxone or test strips or anything else?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And I've watched people walk up and say, can I have that?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: They'll have like a bunch of no-wax and hang.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: They'll say, can I have that kit?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then they're really happy they get to choose.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so it's all about agency.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So I will say while someone may not want to talk at first, they generally do.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: If you say that, you know, it's like neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: When I see the guy who owns the corner store, Mike, on my corner, I'm like, I know him because I've been coming there with my kid for years.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we get to know people over time, and it's the same for syringe redemption.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we do build those relationships.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And that's why, you know, one time I was there and it was like eight degrees out and there was a woman who was a participant who didn't have a maternity coat.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we were able to say, have you been going to San Antonio?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Harm reduction is right down the block and they tend to have the most materials for women of any of the SSPs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so she said, no.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Oh, she said they'd already ordered her coat and they were going to have it for her the next day.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that was because of those ongoing conversations.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And is that typically how a participant ends up moving from redeeming syringes to an ongoing relationship with?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: An SSP, a drop-in center, or not.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: other provider, it sounds like there are opportunities for these warm handoffs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Absolutely, very much.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And it always reminds me of my clinical work and like the kid who would come into my office and sit down and say, I don't want to be here.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And maybe it would be that way for three months.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then in the fourth month, he'd suddenly have something he wanted to tell me about his day.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so having these repeated interactions where people are

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: getting looked at in the eye and getting treated with respect and dignity and interest in who they are and what their lives are really does make it a unique program in terms of being able to engage.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And I would say that of all the harm reduction programs.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, there's a story that Sam from Envoite likes to tell about a participant who got

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: who he called by his actual name and hadn't heard his name uttered in years.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And that is a story that has stuck with me, and it's something that kept him coming back to On Point, so that resonates.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you have a sense of what share of participants are new to the harm reduction system as opposed to people who are already enrolled at On Point?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: At an SSP?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Like, is the CSRP program an effective way to connect with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What's your sense there?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I would say it varies.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I don't know the exact breakdown, but I would say, you know, just from working with New Yorkers that would

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: use programs like this.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Many of them have been in and out of the system so many times, and maybe they've been referred to substance use treatment 12 times.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so each time, you know, for that type of service, there's a barrier.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: You have to do this in order to come or else your case gets closed.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so they're used to cycling through and then slowly becoming someone like that story that Sam tells so eloquently who no one uses your name.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so they will know about the programs usually.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And people also have networks and communities.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so they were hearing about it from the local SSP.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And one of the participants on Monday was sharing that he has been sharing safe disposal information with his neighbors as part of being a participant that he then was able to go out and educate.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So I would say people tend to be aware of the networks, but maybe aren't accessing it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Maybe they're scared that since they, you know, maybe they had an outburst last time they were in a drop-in center, they may not be welcomed back, even though I can say every SSP is fabulous about welcoming you back.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so maybe they just needed another person to say, hey, do you want to walk down the block with me to St.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Anne's Corner of Harm Reduction or Harlem United or whichever the local or vocal, so that they can feel that they can rejoin that community.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to ask a little bit about how some of the other administration's initiatives kind of interplay with DOHMH's strategy to reduce public injection, right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Like, I talked about this in my opening.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The reduction of public injection, sure, we don't want the litter on the streets, but it's a larger issue that we're trying to...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: To address when it comes to people and their needs not being met.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So do you know if the Housing First Initiative is part of DOHMH's strategy to reduce public injection?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And also how are you guys working with DHS and HBD to get people indoors?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, we work incredibly closely with both of those agencies.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I would say regardless of administration, the goal of the health department is to do good public health for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that absolutely means making sure people are getting housing as they need it, making sure we're working with every agency that has access to housing, making sure we're working with the state to figure out are there some additional, like,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: When I started at the health department, there had been a rash of overdose deaths and some supportive housing sites.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so, you know, it was just a natural thing where some people in my bureau were talking to the Bureau of Mental Health and they were figuring out, like, what are the things we need to do?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And do we need to, you know, pilot having one of the peer core trainees go work in supportive housing?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so everyone's trying to use public health to fix the problem.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so I would say, well, it's.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: This administration has been incredibly supportive.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Also, we're just continuing to do public health.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we will always be doing public health.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Capacity always ends up being an issue, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: When CSRP refers to services, do you find that those services have the capacity to take people promptly?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Where are the gaps?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Are people waiting for treatment slots or shelter beds or appointments in particular places?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Can you kind of break down how that's working across different supports or interventions?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, so we're always trying to prioritize the supports where it's, can I walk you down the block or is it next to you?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And that's how I get you to it because this is a population where you really can't be saying, you know, a month from now you can go upstate to this rehab and get a bed.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And maybe if they want that, what are the things I can do with you in this month to help you keep going and keep you safe and alive during this time?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And that's how it operates.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so I would say that people generally get referrals in that moment because that's the type of referral we need.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But is it, how often is that successful?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: How often are you able to say, well, we have an opening, we have an opportunity here, the person is very willing, they want to be connected to something.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: How often is that happening?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Understanding that you're looking for something that's geographically close, that you can do in the moment.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And how often are you like, ugh, missed opportunity because that thing wasn't available?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Because we need more of it.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: More capacity.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So the missed opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: These are more like maybe you showed up at Tuesday at 3 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: When the schedule was Monday at 11 a.m., and then we're trying to do more outreach.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So I would say that's why we partnered so much with the syringe service programs, because they have drop-in centers, and it's so easy to just walk over and access it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's why we try to make it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So I would not say that if someone wants help, they're not going to get it in this program.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Also, it's a small program, and so it's easier to find slots for a small number of people that are right near the thing that they want to access.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'd love to ask you a little bit about workforce and training.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Redemption site staff, are any of them trained as peer or outreach workers?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So they, I would have to check.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I don't think they are certified because the model is trying to offer an access to employment for folks that sometimes...

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: You know, so we work, I would say all the programs add up to workforce support.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so some workforce support for people is that they are ready to go to the OASIS or OMH training.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we send them there and they can get training for that and we can get them certified.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: But sometimes they don't want that yet or they want to see like, what would it be like if I did outreach with Harlem United one afternoon a week?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And that is something they can do with that organization as well.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So we try to offer as many opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Also, the peer core that we have is so that people can do

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Sometimes people have a hard time getting through the certification programs in the time that's set by the state.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we have this program where you can take a little longer to get through it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we're trying to create as many opportunities, whether it's a community health worker or a certified peer.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then sometimes people start as a community health worker and then find out about a certified peer training program, and then they do that too.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then we had someone leave peer core to go to social work school.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we want to make as many opportunities as possible.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What training do Redemption Site staff receive?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So there's really a combination of safety and how to use, say, the microscope to make sure it's a used syringe because we don't want people taking sterile syringes from the pharmacy or wherever they're getting it and then bringing it over to the van.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton

utterances.text: the CSRP spots.

utterances.text: Have any of the SSP, CSRP sites, or peer cleanup teams reported NYPAD activity near their sites while they're out there?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So they try to go to roll call so that they can get to know all of the harm reduction programs do try to go to roll calls and they can get to know the folks in the precinct around.

utterances.text: And so, yeah, on points, a great example, like they were the first to do this and they do a great job of doing that.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so it'll be more of a relationship.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I also will say when the hub stuff started a couple summers ago, that super hot summer, we were all out there trying to figure out.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that was all of the agencies together figuring out, plus all of the outreach folks in the community from DHS, from the substance use treatment programs, from the harm reduction programs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And we were all trying to figure it out together.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's where that came from is if I park on the hub, is that going to help?

utterances.text: Can you steer clear?

utterances.text: And what is happening when they're going to?

utterances.text: And what is happening post roll call?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, so it's going to be a bunch of different things.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: It may be I work on this corner, and so then you know me.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Like, I'm Rebecca.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I'm going to be on this corner, or I'm going to be doing this route.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And if you see me in the community, come say hi.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: If you've noticed someone on your walkthrough that you think could benefit from my services, please, please, please bring them to me.

utterances.text: Also, if maybe there's someone who is someone who is

utterances.text: And so they'll work with NYPD and the officers will say, great, that's fantastic.

utterances.text: And so all together, we're able to figure out what is the approach that's going to help the person.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I mean, the question ultimately is, or the concern ultimately is that if there are police officers hanging around a site that folks are going to be discouraged from participating.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Obviously, there's the other part of this that's like, yeah, you would want a good enough relationship where if a police officer was out, they would proactively reach out to an outreach worker or something and say, hey, you guys go deal with this.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But yeah, I just did.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I don't know that it's totally answered my question about kind of like police activity near the sites or whether that has an impact on participation.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And this is an extreme example.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And we saw that a lot.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I just, yeah, I'm just trying to get a clearer sense of kind of, are they hanging back enough for folks to be able to engage with these teams?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yeah, so that's something that we talk about in our RX stat work that we do across the city and with city and state folks.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: a participant in it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so stigma's there in every field, whether it's substance use treatment or harm reduction or law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we recognize that there's always going to be additional support needed so that someone can be able to see what's the way that's actually going to help in this moment to help this individual rather than like, what are my biases and then how am I acting as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we do do work with all the agencies we talk to, to talk about sort of how is my stigma getting in the way of my being able to effectively engage with someone.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton

utterances.text: And do you have a sense of whether other kind of enforcement policies affect or undermine efforts to connect people to the services, like encampment sweeps, for example?

utterances.text: I would have to defer to other agencies for that.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I don't work with them.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: How effective do you think, do you consider kiosks in reducing syringe litter?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I know I jumped entirely to something else, but I'm curious about that.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: So sometimes they're incredibly effective, and then sometimes we'll notice there hasn't been a single syringe in a kiosk.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we're talking to parks, and we're talking to the community folks, and we're talking to the SSP, and then we're doing education around, hey, did you notice that kiosk?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: I've also been in conversations with parks where they said, oh, we will say to them, you know, no one has been, because we have their data, and we'll say, you know, no one has been accessing this.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then they go find out, oh, it's been covered up by like a bush has grown over it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so then they cut back the bush and then suddenly people are using it again.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so I will say it's a dynamic thing and a conversation rather than how effective, they're tremendously effective overall.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: We just need to make sure people know about them and are using them.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: At the beginning of the hearing, we talked a bit about just the racial disparities.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Overdose deaths are rising fastest among black and Latina New Yorkers.

utterances.text: How are CSRP and the related services, how are they designed to specifically reach those communities?

utterances.text: Yeah, so I'm always conscious of my background, and that's why it was easier for my privilege for me to access the help I needed.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's why we're always trying to make sure that the people we're hiring are representative of the communities they serve.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so I think that's why GUNN is so important.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: government and nonprofit has been so great because we're able to make sure the workforce looks like the people that we're helping.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so I would say that's why we rely on people who have that lived experience to help counsel us on, you know, talking to like National Black Harm Reduction Network and other organizations about like, what are we missing in this approach that we've had?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And then how do we improve things?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Do you have the demographics of the workers?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's what's great about it.

utterances.text: They die at more than twice the rate of Manhattan residents.

utterances.text: Yeah, so that's why our opioid settlement funds and other investments we've made have been targeted in communities.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Every RFP we put out was saying you had to be working and serving communities that were in the highest overdose rate communities because we want to make sure that every dollar we're spending is going to the communities that need it most.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: It is heartbreaking, but also there's a lot of work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so that's why we keep layering on new strategies like adding syringe redemption, adding on additional outreach folks, adding on the recovery centers, adding on additional workforce opportunities for all of those programs as well.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we're constantly trying to layer on for the community.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And in terms of having that workforce represent the community or also just have cultural competency and training and being able to refer to certain types of services,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán

utterances.text: What are the opportunities there for those folks at redemption sites and SSPs?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Yes to all of it.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And as a bisexual New Yorker and a parent of a gay 13-year-old, it's really important for me to make sure that people are taken care of.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And it honestly wouldn't even matter if I were a representative or not.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: Like, these are all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so, for example, like...

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so we want to make sure we have both specializations, and OASIS has a really good designation for treatment programs who are affirming for not just the folks who are coming to see them, but then also for the workforce as well, because that's the key to it really being not stigmatizing.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Lynn Walton
utterances.text: And so there's a long way to go, but I would say we have both trying to make sure the whole workforce is receptive, and then also have those specialization programs that someone just immediately feels safe walking through the front door.
